samples: This program reads a text file, taken from the first command-line argument or a built-in sample path if none is given, and prints the ten most frequent words, each with its count right-aligned beside it. Words are lower-cased and matched case-insensitively, but they are split only on spaces, so punctuation stays attached to words and "word," and "word" are counted separately. It only reads files and writes to the console, and it fails with a file error if the file can't be read. The ordering of words with equal counts isn't specified.

This program reads a text file, taken from the first command-line argument or a built-in sample path if none is given, and counts how often each word appears, ignoring case. It prints the ten most frequent words, one per line, with the count right-aligned before the word. It only reads files and prints to the console, and it fails with a file error if the file can't be read. Words are split on spaces only, so punctuation stays attached ("end." and "end" count separately) and tab-separated words are not split, which makes it better for quick rough counts than for careful text analysis.

This program reads a text file, whose path comes from the first command-line argument or defaults to a sample file, and prints the ten most frequent words. Each line shows the count followed by the word. Words are lower-cased and split only on spaces, so punctuation stays attached ("end." and "end" count separately). The order of words with equal counts isn't specified. It needs console, environment and filesystem-read access, and it fails with a file error if the file can't be read.

This program reads a text file, whose path is given as the first command-line argument (it falls back to a sample file if none is given), and prints the ten most frequent words with their counts. Words are split on spaces and lower-cased, so punctuation stays attached to words and "end." and "end" are counted separately. It only reads files and prints to the console, and it fails with a file error if the file can't be read.

This program reads a text file, whose path comes from the first command-line argument or defaults to a sample file, lowercases the words, counts how often each occurs, and prints the ten most frequent, one per line, with the count right-aligned before the word. It only reads files and prints to the console, and it fails with a file error if the file can't be read. Words are split on spaces only, so punctuation stays attached ("end." and "end" count separately), and the grouping step appears to omit the closing clause that the documented grouping forms always have, so check that it compiles before relying on it.
